concepts.name: SQLite write-ahead logging (WAL)
concepts.reason: The broader WAL system is the parent topic, while this run is limited to checkpointing.

concepts.name: SQLite WAL checkpointing
concepts.reason: This is the single concept the research deepens.

concepts.name: Commit records and checkpoint purpose
concepts.reason: WAL commit records define the changes that checkpointing later transfers.

concepts.name: Reader end marks and checkpoint progress
concepts.reason: Reader end marks constrain which WAL pages a checkpoint can transfer.

concepts.name: Automatic checkpoint scheduling
concepts.reason: Thresholds and connection-close behavior determine when SQLite runs automatic checkpoints.

concepts.name: PASSIVE checkpoint mode
concepts.reason: PASSIVE defines the default non-waiting checkpoint behavior and its limits.

concepts.name: FULL checkpoint mode
concepts.reason: FULL adds specific waiting and writer-blocking behavior.

concepts.name: RESTART checkpoint mode
concepts.reason: RESTART adds a reader condition that lets the next writer restart the WAL.

concepts.name: TRUNCATE checkpoint mode
concepts.reason: TRUNCATE adds zero-length file truncation to RESTART behavior.

concepts.name: NOOP checkpoint mode
concepts.reason: NOOP exposes checkpoint status without checkpointing frames.

concepts.name: Checkpoint locks and busy-handler behavior
concepts.reason: Locks and busy-handler outcomes set the modes' concurrency boundaries.

concepts.name: Checkpoint starvation
concepts.reason: Overlapping readers can prevent checkpoint completion and WAL reset.

concepts.name: Reader gaps
concepts.reason: Reader gaps provide opportunities for a checkpoint to complete.

concepts.name: WAL reset and recycling
concepts.reason: Resetting and recycling control WAL reuse and cleanup.

concepts.name: Large write transactions and checkpoint limits
concepts.reason: A write transaction can prevent WAL reset until the transaction ends.

concepts.name: Checkpoint sync and durability
concepts.reason: Sync ordering and checkpoint placement affect durability.

concepts.name: Checkpoint I/O cost
concepts.reason: Syncs and seek operations contribute to checkpoint cost.

concepts.name: Checkpoint frequency and read/write performance
concepts.reason: Checkpoint frequency trades read performance against write performance.

concepts.name: General WAL reader/writer concurrency and wal-index
concepts.reason: This broader WAL concurrency topic is outside the checkpointing depth boundary.

concepts.name: Rollback-journal commit protocol
concepts.reason: The rollback-journal protocol is a separate journaling approach.

concepts.name: Activating WAL mode
concepts.reason: WAL mode activation is a separate configuration topic.

claims.text: A checkpoint transfers WAL transactions back into the original database.
claims.quote: Moving the WAL file transactions back into the database is called a " checkpoint ".

claims.text: A WAL commit is recorded by appending a commit record and can occur without writing to the original database.
claims.quote: A COMMIT occurs when a special record indicating a commit is appended to the WAL. Thus a COMMIT can happen without ever writing to the original database

claims.text: The default automatic checkpoint threshold is 1000 pages, and a compile-time option can change that default.
claims.quote: By default, SQLite does a checkpoint automatically when the WAL file reaches a threshold size of 1000 pages. (The SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT compile-time option can be used to specify a different default.)

claims.text: A checkpoint running alongside readers stops at a WAL page beyond the end mark of any current reader to avoid overwriting database content that reader uses.
claims.quote: A checkpoint can run concurrently with readers, however the checkpoint must stop when it reaches a page in the WAL that is past the end mark of any current reader.

claims.text: SQLite records checkpoint progress in the wal-index and resumes from that point on the next invocation.
claims.quote: The checkpoint remembers (in the wal-index) how far it got and will resume transferring content from the WAL to the database from where it left off on the next invocation.

claims.text: By default, the commit that pushes the WAL over its size limit runs the checkpoint on the same thread.
claims.quote: By default, the checkpoint will be run automatically by the same thread that does the COMMIT that pushes the WAL over its size limit.

claims.text: A checkpoint usually recycles the WAL by overwriting it from the beginning instead of truncating it.
claims.quote: The checkpoint does not normally truncate the WAL file (unless the journal_size_limit pragma is set). Instead, it merely causes SQLite to start overwriting the WAL file from the beginning.

claims.text: SQLite syncs the WAL before moving its content into the database, then syncs the database before resetting the WAL.
claims.quote: The WAL must be synced to persistent storage prior to moving content from the WAL into the database and the database file must be synced prior to resetting the WAL.

claims.text: The default checkpoint style is PASSIVE and does as much work as possible without interfering with other database connections.
claims.quote: The default checkpoint style is PASSIVE, which does as much work as it can without interfering with other database connections

claims.text: PASSIVE might not finish when readers or writers are concurrent.
claims.quote: The default checkpoint style is PASSIVE, which does as much work as it can without interfering with other database connections, and which might not run to completion if there are concurrent readers or writers.

claims.text: When the last database connection closes, SQLite runs one final checkpoint and deletes the WAL and its associated shared-memory file.
claims.quote: When the last connection to a database closes, that connection does one last checkpoint and then deletes the WAL and its associated shared-memory file, to clean up the disk.

claims.text: FULL waits until there is no writer and all readers use the newest database snapshot, then checkpoints all log frames and syncs the database.
claims.quote: This mode blocks (it invokes the busy-handler callback ) until there is no database writer and all readers are reading from the most recent database snapshot. It then checkpoints all frames in the log file and syncs the database file.

claims.text: FULL blocks new database writers while pending but allows new readers to continue.
claims.quote: This mode blocks new database writers while it is pending, but new database readers are allowed to continue unimpeded.

claims.text: RESTART waits until all readers use only the database file, so the next writer can restart the WAL from the beginning.
claims.quote: after checkpointing the log file it blocks (calls the busy-handler callback ) until all readers are reading from the database file only. This ensures that the next writer will restart the log file from the beginning.

claims.text: TRUNCATE adds truncation of the log file to zero bytes before successful return to RESTART behavior.
claims.quote: This mode works the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART with the addition that it also truncates the log file to zero bytes just prior to a successful return.

claims.text: If another process is checkpointing, the exclusive checkpoint lock cannot be obtained and SQLite returns SQLITE_BUSY without invoking the busy handler.
claims.quote: If any other process is running a checkpoint operation at the same time, the lock cannot be obtained and SQLITE_BUSY is returned. Even if there is a busy-handler configured, it will not be invoked in this case.

claims.text: PASSIVE never invokes the busy-handler callback.
claims.quote: Checkpoint as many frames as possible without waiting for any database readers or writers to finish, then sync the database file if all frames in the log were checkpointed. The busy-handler callback is never invoked in the SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE mode.

claims.text: For FULL, RESTART, and TRUNCATE, a configured busy handler retries obtaining the writer lock if it is not immediately available.
claims.quote: If the writer lock cannot be obtained immediately, and a busy-handler is configured, it is invoked and the writer lock retried until either the busy-handler returns 0 or the lock is successfully obtained.

claims.text: If the busy handler returns 0 while obtaining the writer lock or waiting for readers, the checkpoint proceeds like PASSIVE and returns SQLITE_BUSY.
claims.quote: the checkpoint operation proceeds from that point in the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE - checkpointing as many frames as possible without blocking any further. SQLITE_BUSY is returned in this case.

claims.text: NOOP checkpoints zero frames and exists to expose the values returned through its output parameters.
claims.quote: This mode always checkpoints zero frames. The only reason to invoke a NOOP checkpoint is to access the values returned by sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() via output parameters *pnLog and *pnCkpt.

claims.text: The automatic checkpoint runs after a commit when the WAL has at least N frames.
claims.quote: causes any database on database connection D to automatically checkpoint after committing a transaction if there are N or more frames in the write-ahead log file.

claims.text: Passing zero or a negative N disables automatic checkpoints.
claims.quote: Passing zero or a negative value as the N parameter disables automatic checkpoints entirely.

claims.text: Configuring automatic checkpointing replaces an existing WAL hook, and registering a WAL hook disables that automatic checkpoint mechanism.
claims.quote: The callback registered by this function replaces any existing callback registered using sqlite3_wal_hook() . Likewise, registering a callback using sqlite3_wal_hook() disables the automatic checkpoint mechanism configured by this function.

claims.text: Disabling automatic checkpointing removes the safeguard against excessive WAL growth.
claims.quote: If an application disables the automatic checkpoint, then there is nothing to prevent the WAL file from growing excessively.

claims.text: If overlapping readers always leave at least one active reader, checkpoints cannot complete and the WAL can grow without bound.
claims.quote: However, if a database has many concurrent overlapping readers and there is always at least one active reader, then no checkpoints will be able to complete and hence the WAL file will grow without bound.

claims.text: A reader gap is a period with no database readers during which a checkpoint can be attempted to avoid starvation.
claims.quote: This scenario can be avoided by ensuring that there are "reader gaps": times when no processes are reading from the database and that checkpoints are attempted during those times.

claims.text: A checkpoint cannot complete or reset the WAL in the middle of a write transaction.
claims.quote: A checkpoint can only complete when no other transactions are running, which means the WAL file cannot be reset in the middle of a write transaction.

claims.text: As of SQLite 3.11.0, a single transaction's WAL size should be proportional to the transaction size.
claims.quote: As of SQLite version 3.11.0 (2016-02-15), the WAL file for a single transaction should be proportional in size to the transaction itself.

claims.text: Older SQLite versions could write the same page to the WAL multiple times if a transaction exceeded the page cache.
claims.quote: However, with older versions of SQLite, the same page might be written into the WAL file multiple times if the transaction grows larger than the page cache.

claims.text: With PRAGMA synchronous set to NORMAL, the checkpoint is the only operation that issues an I/O barrier or sync.
claims.quote: Note that with PRAGMA synchronous set to NORMAL, the checkpoint is the only operation to issue an I/O barrier or sync operation (fsync() on unix or FlushFileBuffers() on windows).

claims.text: Running checkpoints in a separate thread or process prevents the main database query and update thread from blocking on a sync operation.
claims.quote: If an application therefore runs checkpoint in a separate thread or process, the main thread or process that is doing database queries and updates will never block on a sync operation.

claims.text: With this separate-checkpoint configuration, transactions might roll back after power failure or a hard reset because they are no longer durable.
claims.quote: The downside to this configuration is that transactions are no longer durable and might rollback following a power failure or hard reset.

claims.text: Checkpoint writes proceed in ascending page order but still have many seek operations interspersed among them.
claims.quote: the pages are transferred from WAL to database in ascending order) but even then there will typically be many seek operations interspersed among the page writes.

claims.text: SQLite states that checkpoints are slower than write transactions.
claims.quote: These factors combine to make checkpoints slower than write transactions. The default strategy is to allow successive write transactions

claims.text: Frequent checkpoints that keep the WAL small maximize read performance.
claims.quote: To maximize the read performance, one wants to keep the WAL as small as possible and hence run checkpoints frequently

claims.text: Infrequent checkpoints maximize write performance by amortizing checkpoint cost across more writes.
claims.quote: To maximize write performance, one wants to amortize the cost of each checkpoint over as many writes as possible
